title: I Watched the Great Pyramid Being Built

narration.text: Egypt. About four and a half thousand years ago.
Fardin is standing on a ramp of mud brick and stone.
Above him, a block of limestone. Two tons. Maybe more.
And it just started sliding.
The workers grab the ropes. They dig in. They stop it.
Just in time.
Most people think slaves built this place. Or aliens.
Nobody here can see him. Nobody would have pulled him out of the way.
Fardin is about to find out the truth.
Because this...
is what they were building.
But let's go back to the beginning.
Giza. On the west bank of the Nile.
The pharaoh Khufu has ordered a tomb bigger than anything the world has ever seen.
This is the Fourth Dynasty, around twenty five sixty BC. Khufu wants it finished in his lifetime.
And everywhere Fardin looks, people are working.
And his watch can jump him forward through the years. So Fardin can watch it rise.
In this episode, Fardin will see three things.
Where these giant stones really came from.
The surprisingly simple trick that moved them.
And what the workers actually ate. That one changes the whole story.
Let's start where every block begins.

graphics.title: COMING UP
items: Where the giant stones came from

narration.text: Every pyramid starts with a hole in the ground.
The core blocks were cut right here, from quarries on the Giza plateau itself.
You can still see those quarries next to the pyramids today.
But for the outer layer, the builders wanted something special.
Brilliant white limestone. From Tura, across the river.

graphics.title: THE QUARRY
graphics.time: Tura · east bank of the Nile

narration.text: No iron. No steel.
Their tools were copper chisels, wooden mallets, and a lot of patience.
Workers cut channels around each block. Then they pried it loose with wooden levers.
Copper is soft. So the chisels had to be sharpened again and again.
It is slow, dusty, deafening work. And Fardin loves every second.

graphics.label: chisels, wooden mallets and levers: no iron tools yet

narration.text: Fardin decides to help.
He grabs a block.
He pulls.
Nothing.
The workers don't even notice. To them, it's just another day at work.
The average block in the Great Pyramid weighs around two and a half tons.
And by one estimate, there are about two point three million of them.

graphics.label: blocks in the Great Pyramid (an estimate)

narration.text: So how do you move a two ton rock across a river?
The answer turned up in the oldest written papyri ever found.
The Nile was Egypt's highway.
Every year the river flooded. And the builders used that water to their advantage.
During the flood, boats could get much closer to Giza. Heavy cargo, less walking.
Fardin tries to hitch a ride. He floats straight through the deck.
Boats carried the stone across the river and along canals, right up to Giza.
In twenty thirteen, archaeologists made an incredible find at Wadi al-Jarf, on the Red Sea coast.
Papyrus scrolls. About forty five hundred years old.
The oldest inscribed papyri ever discovered.
They belonged to an inspector named Merer. And they read like a work diary.
They date to the final years of Khufu's reign.

graphics.title: THE DIARY OF MERER
graphics.sub: Found 2013 at Wadi al-Jarf · oldest known inscribed papyri

narration.text: Merer's logbook tracks his crew of about forty men, hauling limestone from Tura to Giza. By boat.
Load. Sail. Unload. Then back again for more.
Thousands of tons of stone, one boatload at a time.
Not a mystery. Not magic. A schedule, a manager, and a job to do.
But once the stone reached Giza, the real problem began.

graphics.label: in Merer's boat crew, moving Tura limestone to Giza

narration.text: Now the hard part. Getting the stone across the plateau.
No wheels for this job. No cranes.
Blocks were dragged on wooden sledges, pulled by teams with ropes.
Try dragging two tons across dry sand.
The sledge digs in. A pile of sand builds up in front of it.
So someone does something strange.
He pours water on the sand.
Fardin thinks it's a joke.
It isn't.
Wet sand is stiffer. The sledge stops plowing, and starts to glide.
In twenty fourteen, physicists tested this in a lab.
With just the right amount of water, the pulling force dropped by about half.
Too much water, and it gets harder again. It has to be just right.
Egyptians even painted this trick in a tomb. Centuries later.

graphics.label: less pulling force on wet sand (University of Amsterdam, 2014)

narration.text: Simple. Clever. And it works.
Fardin applauds. Nobody hears him.
But the most surprising thing about these workers is still coming.
So who were these workers?
Here is where the story you grew up with falls apart.
For a long time, many people believed they were slaves. Hollywood loved that idea.
Then archaeologists dug up the workers' own town.
It sits just south of the pyramids. Today it's called Heit el-Ghurab.
Archaeologists found bakeries, with stacks of clay bread moulds.
Bread and beer were the everyday food of ancient Egypt.
Fardin can smell the bread. He just can't eat it. Ghost life is hard.

graphics.sub: the pyramid builders' town, south of the plateau

narration.text: And meat. Lots of it.
Researchers found huge numbers of animal bones. Cattle, sheep, and goats.
Some researchers think the animals were raised on farms in the Nile Delta, then brought here.
These workers were well fed.

graphics.label: cattle, sheep and goat bones in huge numbers at the workers' town

narration.text: Work crews had names. Proud ones.
Inside the pyramid, archaeologists found gang names painted on the stones.
One of them was called
Friends of Khufu.
Naming your crew after the king was probably a point of pride.
And when a worker got hurt, someone took care of him.
Skeletons from the workers' cemetery show broken bones that healed properly. That means medical care.
Somebody here cared whether these people lived.

graphics.label: broken bones set and healed: evidence of medical care

narration.text: Then came the biggest clue of all.
The workers were buried in their own tombs, right beside the pyramids. Near their king.
Most archaeologists say that is not how you treat slaves.
Many were probably farmers, working in rotating crews, paid in food.
Thousands of them. Skilled, organised Egyptian workers.

graphics.fact: Fed, organised Egyptian workers, buried near their king

narration.text: Fardin twists his watch. Months fly by. Then years.
Season after season, the pyramid rises.
Each new layer is a little smaller than the one below. The top creeps closer every year.
But how did they get the blocks all the way up there?

graphics.label: to build it: the traditional estimate

narration.text: Honest answer?
Scholars still debate it.
A long straight ramp? A ramp spiralling around the outside? Some even suggest a ramp inside the pyramid.
Every idea has problems. A straight ramp to the top would have to be enormous.
One real clue turned up in twenty eighteen, at an ancient quarry called Hatnub.
A steep ramp, with a staircase on each side and rows of post holes for hauling ropes.
Teams could pull blocks up a slope much steeper than anyone expected.
And it dates to the reign of Khufu.

graphics.label: a ramp system from Khufu's reign, found in 2018

narration.text: Up here, every mistake is dangerous.
A rope slips.
The block slides back. The team digs in.
They hold it.
Fardin's heart is pounding. He's a ghost, and he still ducked.
Thousands of blocks. Every single day. For about twenty years.
At night, the crews rest by the fire.
Fardin looks up. The stars over Giza are blazing.
And the finished pyramid will not look like the one you know.
The final step. The casing stones.
Polished white Tura limestone, fitted over every side. Smooth as glass.
Each casing stone was cut at an angle, so all four sides became perfect smooth slopes.
And when the sun hit it...
it shone.
Like a giant mirror in the desert.
About one hundred and forty six metres tall. The tallest human-made structure on Earth.
Its base covers more than five hectares. That's about seven football fields.
And it stayed the tallest for nearly four thousand years.

graphics.label: original height (481 ft) of Khufu's pyramid

marks.label: AD 1311 · LINCOLN CATHEDRAL TAKES THE RECORD

graphics.caption: Tallest human-made structure for nearly 4,000 years

narration.text: Fardin climbs to the very top.
Below him, the green ribbon of the Nile valley. Beyond it, endless desert.
Today, most of that white casing is gone. Much of it was carried away for other buildings, centuries later.
But for a while, this was the brightest thing in the desert.

graphics.text: CASING LATER REMOVED FOR BUILDING STONE

narration.text: And here is the strangest part.
Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing...
than to the building of this pyramid.

graphics.caption: Cleopatra → Moon landing: about 2,000 years. Pyramid → Cleopatra: about 2,500.

narration.text: Then Fardin's watch glitches.
The ground starts to shake.
And far away, a mountain is smoking.
Fardin has a very bad feeling about this.
Next stop...
Pompeii.
Subscribe, or Fardin stays lost in time.

graphics.sub: or Fardin stays lost in time
